Narrowing the jack mackerel CMP comparison

Working paper: best-relative scorecards, management trade-offs and matched simulation trajectories

Published

September 8, 2026

Back to the jack mackerel wiki · All eight CMPs: best-relative scorecard · Three retained CMPs: best-relative scorecard

NoteStatus and scope

This is a working comparison for discussion, not an agreed CMP selection or a new assessment. It uses the saved 500-simulation outputs, with no retuning or changes to operating models. Screening narrows the reference-OM presentation; robustness results remain separate and can justify reinstating an omitted CMP. The full set remains available in the scorecard and downloadable data.

1 Findings for discussion

Three CMPs provide a compact view of the main management choices: HS−20 (MP43), HS−30 (MP47), and PR−20 (MP44). HS−20 represents the lower-variability hockey-stick alternatives with a 20% advice-reduction limit. HS−30 retains the contrast offered by allowing larger reductions. PR−20 retains the higher-catch power-ramp alternative and its greater interannual variability.

This selection is a presentation screen with explicit tolerances, not a demonstration that every excluded CMP is inferior. Small differences in reference-OM indicators are treated as close alternatives. Two cases are less favourable within the specified tolerances; their remaining advantages are stated below. No minimum acceptable risk level has been agreed or applied here, and a best-relative score of 100 does not establish acceptability.

2 Data, periods and indicator definitions

The source set contains eight CMPs, each with 500 simulations under the reference OM and nine robustness OMs. Two-stock OMs are shown by biological component; their catches and biomasses are not silently pooled. All performance calculations in this paper use 2041–2050, except the inherited mean-catch-reduction column available as an optional scorecard indicator, which uses 2026–2050. The worm plots span 2025–2050.

For catch, interannual catch change (IACC), and SSB/SSBMSY, first calculate each simulation’s mean over 2041–2050. Trade-off points then show the median across 500 simulations; horizontal and vertical bars show the 25th–75th percentiles. The bars describe simulation variation, not confidence intervals for the median. IACC is the absolute percentage change from the previous year’s realized catch. The 2041 change therefore uses catch in 2040. The biomass ratio in the trade-off plots uses the stored static SSBMSY denominator; it is distinct from the dynamic-B0 risk indicator.

The low-biomass indicator is the proportion of simulation-years with SSB <8% of the matching year’s dynamic B0, the previous Blim. Dynamic B0 is the saved projected unfished SSB for the matching simulation. Each year below the threshold counts, including consecutive years. Catch below 270 kt is also a pooled simulation-year frequency.

The filtered catch-cut count counts retained realized-catch reductions greater than 20.1%. Transitions are excluded when SSB is below 8% of dynamic B0 in either the current or previous year, or the reduction is within 0.1 percentage point of 20%. These are diagnostic exclusions requested for this indicator only: the low-SSB indicator, catch and IACC trade-offs, and worm plots retain the crash trajectories. A wholly excluded window has zero retained events. The plotted mean count is per original ten-year simulation window, not a conditional probability of a cut among eligible years. Recorded advice respects the 20% limit within numerical tolerance in the checked HS−20 run; realized-catch shortfalls and numerical edge cases motivated the filter. It does not certify every projection as numerically sound.

Annual exclusion diagnostics and counts and eligible years per simulation retain the audit trail.

3 Screening the CMP set

Five management-facing indicators are used for this screen: median catch, IACC, low-catch probability, SSB-below-previous-Blim frequency, and the filtered catch-cut count. All eleven indicators remain available in the scorecards; the screening is deliberately not an eleven-indicator dominance claim.

The following absolute differences are treated as small for this exploratory presentation screen, not as adopted management tolerances:

Indicator Screening tolerance Preferred direction
Median catch 40 thousand t Higher
IACC 0.6 percentage point Lower
Probability of catch below 270 kt 1 percentage point Lower
Frequency below previous Blim 1 percentage point Lower
Filtered catch-cut count 0.1 event per ten-year window Lower

A close alternative differs from its retained comparator by no more than every listed tolerance. A poorer performer within these tolerances has a retained comparator that is no worse beyond any tolerance and better beyond at least one. Every omitted CMP is compared directly with a retained CMP; there is no chain of eliminations. Choosing HS−20 and PR−20 as the representatives preserves the focal minus-20 variants for discussion. It is a declared editorial choice, not the result of optimizing a composite score.

CMP Disposition Representative
HS+20 Close alternative HS-20
HSsym Close alternative HS-20
PR+20 Poorer within screening tolerances HS-20
PRsym Close alternative PR-20
PR-30 Poorer within screening tolerances HS-30

HS+20 retains a modest biomass advantage over HS−20, and HSsym has slightly lower IACC. PRsym has slightly lower IACC than PR−20 but lower catch. These distinctions remain visible in the full scorecard. PR+20 has markedly greater IACC than its HS−20 comparator while catch is close. PR−30 has a lower low-catch frequency than HS−30, but by less than the one-percentage-point screening tolerance; it has substantially higher IACC and more filtered large cuts. Thus “poorer” here means poorer under these five indicators and tolerances in the reference OM, not universally inferior across OMs, metrics, or stakeholder preferences.

4 Scorecards: best 100, others relative to it

Use the all-eight-CMP scorecard to review the original set and the retained-set scorecard for the three-way comparison. Both open with best-relative scaling and equal weights on the five screening indicators. Users can change CMPs, indicators, scaling and weights. The aggregate score is illustrative; it is not used to generate the shortlist.

For a higher-is-better indicator, the score is \(100V_i/\max_j(V_j)\). For a lower-is-better indicator, it is \(100\min_j(V_j)/V_i\). The best value therefore scores 100. Scores are recalculated for the selected CMP set, so scores from different selections should not be compared as though their reference were fixed.

Zero-best exception: when the best value for a lower-is-better indicator is zero, zero-valued CMPs score 100 and positive-valued CMPs score zero. This rule is necessary because the ordinary ratio cannot distinguish positive values when its numerator is zero. All three retained CMPs are not tied on the filtered-cut count: HS−20 and PR−20 are zero, while HS−30 is positive. Giving this column a substantial weight can therefore impose a sharp penalty. Inspect its raw count and the exclusion definitions before assigning weight. Equal weights also do not remove overlap between related stock or stability indicators.

The existing general best-relative explorer and original range-scaled explorer provide the broader application context. The two companion scorecards above embed this paper’s exact data snapshot for reproducibility.

5 Reference-OM trade-offs after screening

The reference plots expose the cost of concentrating on one outcome. More stable catches, higher catch and lower depletion risk need not select the same CMP. Overlapping simulation ranges are expected and do not erase paired differences between rules. The shortlist should be revisited if a different time horizon, screening tolerance or biological constraint is agreed.

6 Does the contrast persist under alternative OMs?

The reference screen is not automatically generalized to robustness OMs. The following plots keep each OM and stock component separate. Panel scales vary to make within-panel comparisons legible; compare numerical axes before comparing distances across panels. No probabilities or weights have been assigned to the OMs.

Among the retained CMPs, PR−20 has the highest median catch in the reference and alternative-selectivity OMs, while one of the hockey-stick CMPs has the higher catch in the other non-collapsed panels. PR−20 often retains a higher SSB/static-SSBMSY ratio under robustness OMs. These contrasts reinforce the need to consider yield and biomass jointly rather than extrapolating the reference-OM ranking. The northern component of h2_1.14 has essentially zero catch under all three CMPs; that panel is labelled and not interpreted as a meaningful ranking. Its raw values remain in the downloadable data.

All eight CMPs’ OM-specific summaries are retained in the complete trade-off data. An omitted CMP should be reinstated if the working group identifies a material robustness advantage not captured by the reference screen. This paper does not declare an across-OM winner, and its tolerance-based screening is not a statistical test of equivalence or dominance.

7 Fifteen matched simulation worms

The 15 iteration IDs are reused from the earlier paired reference figure: 37, 65, 110, 151, 158, 165, 177, 186, 246, 327, 344, 348, 367, 397 and 498. The same IDs and colours are used in all six panels. They were not reselected to favour the retained CMPs or remove poor trajectories. Matching an iteration ID preserves the posterior-draw comparison; this alone does not establish identical stochastic observation innovations across differently seeded CMP tuning runs.

These worms illustrate timing, persistence and contrasting paths, not the probability of an outcome. They represent 15 of 500 simulations and are not uncertainty envelopes. The full-distribution trade-off summaries and low-biomass frequencies remain the basis for comparing typical performance and risk.

8 Decisions this paper can support

  1. Review the explicit screening tolerances and decide whether the three-CMP presentation set is sufficient for the next discussion.
  2. Set biological acceptability criteria separately from best-relative scoring; a relatively high score can coexist with unacceptable risk.
  3. Examine robustness panels and the full-set data before treating an omitted CMP as dispensable.
  4. Agree which indicators and weights represent the objectives, paying particular attention to zero-best risk indicators and overlapping measures.
  5. Retain projection-failure diagnostics and advice-versus-realized-catch checks as outstanding validation work. The filtered catch-cut statistic does not repair a failed projection or remove its consequences from other indicators.

9 Reproducibility and scope of validation

The new script R/build_cmp_screening_paper.R reads the saved reference and robustness performance tables from output/candidate-performance-500/, and the reference runs from jmMSE-500-refine/model/tune/refine_500_from_100/runs.rds. No simulations were rerun. The current quilt supplies the filtered catch-cut and dynamic-B0 risk values. Input checksums and the R session are recorded in provenance. This paper’s editable Quarto source and companion data permit revision without editing the displayed figures manually.

Validation checks require 500 iterations for every OM/CMP/component summary, complete 15-by-26-year worm panels, common worm IDs, documented mass units, and direct numerical confirmation of every screening comparison. The HTML uses semantic headings and tables, numerical data alternatives, captions, and figure descriptions. Screen-reader testing and formal accessibility certification have not been performed. Saved model dynamics and reference-point conventions are inherited; this is an output-analysis paper, not a new verification of the assessment or projection solver.
